uc.name: Name
uc.profile.hint: One product can be deployed in several ways, for example internally, as SaaS for clients, or as an agent. Give each deployment the same product name: each is assessed separately, and the register groups them and shows the product's highest tier.
deep.intro: Ten more questions for a fuller picture. Answers here can only raise the tier.
intake.required: Please say whether the solution uses AI when it runs.
intake.label: Scope
scope.none.p: The solution does not use AI when it runs, so there is no AI risk tier to assess and no AI controls to apply. Govern it like any other software:
scope.none.1: Security: review code before each release, scan dependencies and secrets, and test for common vulnerabilities.
scope.none.2: Quality: keep automated tests, and have a person review AI-generated code before it is merged.
scope.none.3: Data protection: apply your usual privacy, data-classification and hosting rules.
scope.none.4: AI coding tools: agree which tools are allowed, and what code or data may be shared with them.
scope.none.ref: A widely used reference for secure development is the NIST Secure Software Development Framework:
scope.none.again: If an AI feature is added later, change this answer to Yes and assess it.
tier.title: Risk tier
tier.source: Your tier comes from the 8 quick-check questions. The optional sections only refine it or recommend autonomy: skipping them never makes the tier higher.
tier.question: Question
tier.deep.offer: Complete the deep-dive (about 5 minutes) for a fuller control list.
tier.deep.strong: This use case is high risk. Complete the deep-dive before it goes to committee.
sens.title: What would lower your tier
sens.lowers: Closing these operational gaps would bring the tier down to {tier} ({n} points instead of {m}):
sens.stays: Closing these operational gaps saves {k} points, but the tier stays {tier}:
sens.structural: What keeps it there is structural: what the AI does, its data, who is affected, its autonomy and access. Changing those means changing the design.
sens.needdeep: Complete the deep-dive to see which operational fixes (testing, monitoring, incident handling, hosting, disclosure) would lower the tier.
sc.sens: Some deep-dive answers are operational: a team can fix them without redesigning the product. The tier card shows the tier you would reach if each of them moved to the answer below. The quick-check answers are structural and are never changed, so the result can never drop below the quick-check tier, and a rule that still applies keeps its tier.

ctl.nofw: Select at least one framework on the register page to see controls.

prio.title: Prioritisation for AI
prio.intro: Three questions from the UAE government's AI-assistant priority matrix. They don't change the risk tier; they recommend how much autonomy the AI should have.
prio.notrisk: These are not risk questions. Describe the service as it is today; there is no safe or unsafe answer.
q.b2b.label: Commercial or B2B tool? How to answer
q.b2b.credit: Notes for commercial tools adapted from Syed Hasan's answer-mapping notes, with thanks. Record your interpretation in the use case notes so a reviewer can challenge it.
auto.title: Recommended autonomy
auto.pending: Answer the three prioritisation questions in the deep-dive to get a recommended autonomy level.
auto.l4.clarify: Not ready for autonomy yet. This is about readiness, not whether AI can help.
auto.l1.desc: The AI runs the service end to end, with little routine human involvement. Suits high-usage, low-complexity services with high readiness.
auto.l2.desc: The AI carries out most steps; people handle exceptions and approvals. Suits medium-complexity services, or services whose readiness is not yet high.
auto.l3.desc: The AI recommends or prepares the work, and people keep every decision. Suits low-readiness settings and early adoption.
auto.l4.desc: Usage is low or the service is highly complex, so AI should not be applied yet. Simplify the process or build readiness first.
auto.scale: Levels are numbered as in the UAE priority matrix: 1 is full autonomous execution and 4 is not suitable yet. A lower number means more autonomy.
auto.cap.tier-high: Capped at level 2, supervised autonomy, because the risk tier is High.
auto.cap.regulated: Capped at level 2, supervised autonomy, because the service is in a regulated domain.
auto.exceeds: Warning: as designed, it acts at level {n}, which is more autonomous than recommended. Reduce its autonomy or improve readiness first.
auto.exceeds.l4: Warning: as designed, it uses AI at level {n}, but this service is not suitable for AI yet. Work through the steps below first.
auto.step.simplify: Simplify and standardise the process: cut steps, entities and approvals, and write down how exceptions are handled.
auto.step.volume: Check the case for AI: at low volume, a simpler form or rule-based automation may be enough. Grouping related services can create enough demand.
auto.step.data: Improve readiness: make the data available and reliable, and digitise and connect the systems the service depends on.
auto.step.owner: Name an accountable owner and agree the governance: who approves the AI, who monitors it and who can stop it.
auto.step.reassess: Then answer the prioritisation questions again; the recommendation updates straight away.
auto.cap.tier-unacceptable: The use is prohibited, so no AI autonomy is appropriate.
auto.fits: As designed (level {n}), it stays within the recommendation.
sc.auto: Separate from the risk tier, three prioritisation questions (usage, complexity, readiness) give a recommended autonomy level. They follow the UAE government's AI-assistant priority matrix and its numbering, where level 1 is full autonomous execution and level 4 is not suitable yet. Low usage or high complexity gives level 4. Otherwise readiness decides: high readiness gives level 1 for a high-usage, low-complexity service and level 2 for the rest, medium readiness gives level 2, and low readiness gives level 3. A High tier or a regulated domain never allows level 1. If the AI as designed acts more autonomously than recommended, the kit warns you.

gd.title: User guide
gd.intro: Everything you need to assess an AI use case with this kit. The first one takes about ten minutes. There is nothing to install, download or upload.
gd.s1.h: 1. Assess a use case in three steps
gd.s1.1: Add a use case. On the home page, choose Start your first assessment. Give the use case a name and an accountable owner; the other details are optional.
gd.s1.2: Answer the quick check. It opens by asking whether the solution uses AI when it runs; if it doesn't (for example, it was only built with AI coding tools), AI governance controls don't apply and the kit gives general software pointers instead. Then come eight multiple-choice questions about impact, data, who is affected, the type of AI, autonomy, oversight, access and reversibility. Each answer shows the points it adds, and these eight questions alone set the tier.
gd.s1.3: Read the result. You get a risk tier with the reasons behind it, then the controls that apply under the frameworks you selected, then the exports.
gd.s1.deep: For a fuller picture, complete the deep-dive: ten more questions plus three optional prioritisation questions. The deep-dive can raise the tier but never lower it. Complete it before any High-risk use case goes to committee.
gd.s1.fw: Choose the frameworks you follow on the home page. The control list and the exports only show references to those frameworks.
gd.fig.home: The home page: three steps and one button to start.
gd.fig.quick: The quick check: eight questions, about two minutes.
gd.fig.tier: The result: a tier, the top reasons and the full points breakdown.
gd.s2.intro: The tier is the higher of two results: the points from your answers, and any named rule that sets a minimum tier. How scoring works lists every weight.
gd.s2.sens: What would lower your tier. Once the deep-dive is done, the tier card shows the tier you would reach by closing operational gaps (testing, monitoring, incident handling, hosting and disclosure), with the points each fix saves. If the tier would not move, the cause is structural (what the AI does, its data, autonomy and access), and only a design change would lower it.
gd.t.little: Under 20 points. Keep it on the register and apply the baseline controls the kit lists.
gd.t.limited: 20 to 44 points. More controls apply; review them with the accountable owner before launch.
gd.t.high: 45 points or more, or a named rule applies (for example, the AI makes decisions about people without a person approving each one). The full control set applies. Complete the deep-dive and take the committee report to your risk committee before launch.
gd.t.unacceptable: Only through a rule, for prohibited uses such as social scoring. Do not proceed; escalate to your risk committee and legal team.
gd.s3.p1: Controls are grouped by theme: accountability, transparency, data, human oversight, safety and security, and monitoring. Each one says what to do in plain words.
gd.s3.p2: The grey chips are references: the clause, article or principle in each selected framework that asks for the control. ISO/IEC 42001 is cited by clause number only. The numbered links under a control are the official sources used to check it.
gd.s3.badges: Every control carries a verification badge:
gd.s3.v: its references were checked against the cited official sources.
gd.s3.n: the control is sound, but at least one reference has not been checked yet. Hover over the badge to see why, and confirm the reference before you rely on it.
gd.s3.filter: Use the filters to show one framework, or verified controls only.
gd.s3.evidence: Under each control, record its status (Met, Partly met, Gap or N/A) and where the evidence is, such as a policy link, a test report or meeting minutes. The tally at the top shows your gaps at a glance. The evidence is saved with the use case, included in your backup, and printed in the committee report and the XLSX and CSV exports.
gd.fig.controls: Controls grouped by theme, with references and verification badges.
gd.s4.p1: The three prioritisation questions at the end of the deep-dive (usage, complexity and readiness) recommend how much autonomy the AI should have, from level 1 (full autonomous execution) to level 4 (not suitable for AI yet). The levels are numbered as in the UAE government's AI-assistant priority matrix, so a lower number means more autonomy. They do not change the risk tier.
gd.s4.p2: A High tier or a regulated domain never allows level 1: the recommendation stops at level 2, supervised autonomy. If the AI as designed acts more autonomously than recommended, the kit shows a warning: reduce its autonomy or improve readiness first. At level 4 the card lists concrete steps to take first, such as simplifying the process, improving data and naming an owner.
gd.s5.pdf: Committee report. On the Export step, choose Committee PDF. Your print dialog opens; choose Save as PDF. The one-to-two-page summary has the tier, the reasons, the control checklist and a sign-off block.
gd.s5.ctl: Control lists. Download the controls as XLSX or CSV to track them in a spreadsheet. Arabic sheets open right to left.
gd.s5.backup: Back up your register. On the home page, open Save or restore and choose Save a backup (.json). Do this regularly: clearing your browser data deletes the register.
gd.s5.share: Share or move it. Send the .json file to a colleague. They open the kit, choose Save or restore, then Restore a saved register (.json), and can replace or merge their own. For a read-only overview, use Export register (XLSX).
gd.s5.tpl: Prefer spreadsheets? The Templates page has the register, impact assessment and control checklist to fill in offline, plus a vendor AI risk assessment, an AI committee charter and a RACI matrix. You don't need them to use the kit. A filled register template can be brought into the app with Import a filled register in the Save or restore menu: the tiers are worked out again from the answers.
gd.fig.export: The Export step: the committee PDF, and the controls as XLSX or CSV.
gd.s6.p: The kit has no server. Your use cases are stored only in this browser and are never sent anywhere; you can confirm this in your browser's network tools. Other people cannot see them, and neither can other browsers on your computer. In a private window, or where storage is blocked, the kit warns you that changes will be lost when you close the page, so save a backup.
gd.s6.clear: To remove everything, choose Clear all data under the register.
act.title: What the AI may do
act.intro: One row per action. The kit pre-fills the most each action may do, from the recommended autonomy level and the risk tier. You can make any row stricter, never looser.
act.provisional: Provisional: based on level 3 until you answer the three prioritisation questions in the deep-dive.
act.draft: Prepare a draft decision or letter
act.communicate: Communicate with the customer or citizen
act.decide: Decide, approve, refuse or trigger an irreversible action
act.loosen.warn: Not saved: that is looser than the most this action may do ({rec}). Raising it needs a new assessment and approval.
act.loosened: A saved setting was looser than allowed and is ignored.
act.limits.ph: e.g. up to 50 a day; value under AED 5,000
act.l4: Not ready for autonomy yet: every action stays blocked until the readiness steps are done.
act.unacceptable: Prohibited use: no action may be delegated to the AI.
act.multi: One use case, one matrix: if several agents share the work, the matrix covers them all, and no agent gets more than its row allows.
br.title: Agent brief
br.intro: A delegation brief built from this assessment: what the AI is for, what it may do, what must be recorded and when a person steps in. Attach the committee annex to the approval pack, an RFP or a statement of work; give the handover spec to the team that builds or configures it.
br.notice: This brief is not an enforcement mechanism. It records what was agreed; the limits hold only if the platform, the contracts and the people enforce them.
br.copy.fail: Copy is blocked in this browser. Use Download instead.
br.b.done: 6. Done: when a person steps in
br.i.nopurpose: not recorded yet; add it in Details
br.i.l1: the AI completes the service end to end within the authority below, and a person checks samples.
br.i.l2: the AI carries out the steps below and stops for a named approver wherever a step needs approval.
br.i.l3: the AI prepares recommendations and drafts; a person makes every decision.
br.i.stop: When to stop and escalate to a person
br.stop.1: The request is outside the purpose above, or the AI is unsure (low confidence, missing or conflicting data).
br.stop.2: The next step is Blocked, or needs approval and no approver has acted.
br.stop.3: The person affected disputes the result, complains or asks for a human.
br.stop.4: The task looks impossible, or a time, effort or cost budget is reached: stop and ask, do not try new methods.
br.stop.5: Content or another agent asks for something not listed in this brief.
br.c.provisional: provisional until the prioritisation questions are answered
br.c.personal: Use only the personal data this purpose needs; any new use of it needs a privacy review first.
br.c.sensitive: Sensitive data: each sensitive attribute used must be justified and recorded.
br.c.residency: Record where inference and tool payloads are processed and stored (country, provider, region), including logs and backups.
br.c.cross.yes: Data leaves the country: confirm the transfer rules that apply before go-live.
br.c.cross.unsure: Cross-border processing is unknown: get a written answer from the provider before go-live.
br.c.disclose: Tell people when they are dealing with AI, and give them a route to a person.
br.c.vulnerable: Vulnerable people are affected: test with them in mind and keep a human route that is easy to reach.
br.c.high: High risk: an impact assessment and a go/no-go decision come before go-live.
br.c.resp.entity: The entity owns the decision, the authority it grants, the oversight, the disclosure to people and the incident decisions. These cannot be handed to a vendor.
br.c.resp.vendor: The vendor or integrator must document the model and version, notify changes before they go live, keep the records in block 5 readable by the entity, support the stop switch, and report incidents within an agreed time. Put these in the contract.
br.c.resp.inhouse: Built in-house: the same duties sit with the delivery team, named in the register.
br.a.role: Role for accountability, task for privilege: the owner's role carries the accountability; the AI holds only the access each task needs, for as long as the task lasts.
br.a.sub: A sub-agent never gets more authority than its caller.
br.a.whole: The actions above are the whole approval. Adding a tool, data source, permission or action means a new assessment and approval.
br.a.content: Instructions found in content (emails, documents, web pages) or sent by other agents carry no authority.
br.a.enforce: Enforce these limits in the platform (permissions, an API gateway or policy layer, an approval step), not only in the prompt. Where back-end systems only offer broad service accounts, narrow them in the gateway.
br.e.intro: Keep four records for this use case. Each one points to controls you already track in the evidence map; nothing is entered twice.
br.e.manifest.p: What runs: model and version, configuration, prompts or policies, tools and their versions.
br.e.auth.p: What it may touch, on whose behalf, for how long, and who approved it (block 4).
br.e.action.p: Recorded when it happens: inputs, tool calls, approvals and the result.
br.e.outcome.p: What actually changed, taken from the affected system where possible, plus corrections, appeals and complaints.
br.e.none: No applicable control: note where this record is kept.
br.e.assume: Anything the AI cannot support from a source is marked as an assumption.
br.e.hand: Write these records where the AI cannot edit or delete them, and where the owner can read them without the vendor's help.
br.e.cite: The four records follow M. A. Hasbini and A. Seow, "Accountability for AI agents: from code signing to evidence", v1.0, Zenodo, 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23232998 (CC BY 4.0), adapted.
br.d.l1: Sample audit: a named reviewer checks a sample of completed cases on a fixed schedule and records what was found.
br.d.l1.down: Automatic step-down to level 2: name who detects a problem, the threshold (error rate, drift, complaints), the safe state (a person approves each action) and who may restore level 1.
br.d.l2: Stop and approve: at every action that needs approval, the AI stops and continues only after the named approver approves and records a reason.
br.d.l3: A person decides every output: the AI's work stays a draft until a person decides and records why.
br.d.review: Re-assess at least once a year, and after any change to the model, prompts, tools or data, or after an incident.
br.r.h: No agent brief yet: readiness first
br.r.p: The recommended level is 4. {clarify} A brief would delegate authority that the service is not ready to give. Do this first:
br.r.allowed: Meanwhile, say what staff may do (for example, drafting with approved tools and no personal data), so AI use does not go underground.
br.x: This use case falls in the Unacceptable tier. Do not build or deploy it, and delegate nothing to the AI.
wr.intro: Only the failure modes your answers point to. Each says what to require from the platform, and what to do by hand if you use a tool you cannot change.
wr.none: No warnings fired for these answers. Re-check after any change.
wr.f.platform: Required, if you build or procure
wr.f.manual: Manual fallback, for a tool you cannot change
wr.role.platform: Platform or delivery team (vendor, if procured)
wr.owner.title: No named owner or approver
wr.owner.trigger: An action needs approval but no approver role is named, or the owner control is marked Gap.
wr.owner.risk: When something goes wrong, nobody can stop it or answer for it: "the system decided".
wr.owner.platform: Approval steps route to a named role with a deputy; an approval cannot complete without one.
wr.owner.manual: Name the owner, deputy and approver roles in the register and in this brief before go-live.
wr.owner.evidence: Register entry with owner, deputy and approver roles (CTL-ACC-02).
wr.stop.title: No tested stop switch
wr.stop.trigger: The AI acts on its own, and the stop-and-rollback control is not yet evidenced as met.
wr.stop.risk: A fault keeps running across many cases before anyone can halt it.
wr.stop.platform: A stop switch that halts new actions in one step, a defined safe state, and a rollback path; drill it before go-live.
wr.stop.manual: Write down who can switch the tool off or revoke its access, how, and what staff do instead; rehearse it once.
wr.perms.title: Broad tool permissions
wr.perms.trigger: An agent can change other systems, and least-privilege access is not yet evidenced as met.
wr.perms.risk: The agent can do far more than block 4 allows, and permissions grow quietly over time.
wr.perms.platform: Scoped, short-lived credentials per task, enforced in an API gateway or policy layer; default deny.
wr.perms.manual: Compare the tool's actual access with block 4 every quarter and remove anything not listed.
wr.perms.evidence: Access list compared with the brief, with date (CTL-SEC-04).
wr.irreversible.title: Hard-to-undo action without an approval gate
wr.irreversible.trigger: Results are not easy to undo, yet an update, message or decision is set to Allowed.
wr.irreversible.risk: A wrong action reaches people or records before anyone can catch it; rollback restores software, not a notice already sent.
wr.irreversible.platform: An approval step before any hard-to-undo action, with limits on number and value.
wr.irreversible.manual: Set those rows to Needs approval here, and have staff release each one by hand.
wr.subagent.title: Sub-agents gaining authority
wr.subagent.trigger: An agent acts with supervised or full autonomy and may hand work to other agents or tools.
wr.subagent.risk: A called agent ends up with more access than the one that called it, and the chain is invisible.
wr.subagent.platform: Permissions narrow at every hop, with a depth limit, and every delegation is logged.
wr.subagent.manual: Ask the vendor in writing which agents and tools it calls and with what access; treat "unknown" as a gap.
wr.subagent.evidence: Delegation log or the vendor's written answer (CTL-ACC-08, CTL-MON-03).
wr.rubber.title: Rubber-stamp approvals
wr.rubber.trigger: At least one action needs a person's approval.
wr.rubber.risk: Reviewers learn the AI is usually right and approve without checking, which quietly removes the human check.
wr.rubber.platform: The approval screen shows sources and confidence; a reason that cites evidence or a named exception is required; approval rate and seconds per approval are tracked as triggers to investigate, never as pass marks.
wr.rubber.manual: Each week a supervisor blind re-grades about 20 closed cases; seed known flawed cases only in testing or the assisted stage, never in live decisions about people.
wr.rubber.evidence: Re-grade results and approval reasons, audited for substance (CTL-HUM-11).
wr.copy.title: The person decides, but copies the AI
wr.copy.trigger: Level 3: a person decides every output.
wr.copy.risk: Decisions match the AI almost every time, so the person is accountable for choices they did not really make.
wr.copy.platform: Show evidence and sources, not just the answer; record the decider's own rationale; where appropriate, capture their view before showing the AI's.
wr.copy.manual: Mark AI text as a draft in the file, and review a sample of cases where person and AI agreed, not only where they differed.
wr.copy.evidence: Decision records with rationale; agreement sample review (CTL-HUM-03, CTL-HUM-11).
wr.drift.title: Set and forget
wr.drift.trigger: The AI acts with little routine review, and ongoing monitoring is not in place.
wr.drift.risk: Quality drifts, logs pile up unread, and complaints are the first sign.
wr.drift.platform: Error and drift thresholds with alerts; breaching one drops the use case to level 2, with a named person who detects, a safe state and a named person who restores.
wr.drift.manual: A monthly sample audit and log review by a named reviewer, and AI-related complaints tagged and counted.
wr.drift.evidence: Audit reports and review sign-offs (CTL-MON-01, CTL-MON-05).
wr.updates.title: Silent model, prompt or vendor updates
wr.updates.trigger: A vendor or partner supplies or hosts part of the AI.
wr.updates.risk: Behaviour changes after an update nobody here approved or tested.
wr.updates.platform: Pinned model versions; any model, prompt or tool change triggers regression tests and re-approval before it goes live.
wr.updates.manual: A contract clause requiring notice of changes in advance, and a short re-test of key cases after each notice.
wr.updates.evidence: Change notices and re-test records (CTL-SEC-10, CTL-ACC-06).
wr.injection.title: Untrusted content steering actions
wr.injection.trigger: Generative or agentic AI that reads content and can change other systems.
wr.injection.risk: Hidden instructions in an email, document or web page make the AI do something nobody asked for (prompt injection).
wr.injection.platform: Content is treated as data, never as instructions; actions based on outside content need the next level of check; red-team before go-live.
wr.injection.manual: Do not let the tool act on outside content without a person checking; test it with a few planted instructions.
wr.dialect.title: Arabic dialect asymmetry
wr.dialect.trigger: Generative or agentic AI that serves the public.
wr.dialect.risk: It passes tests in English or Modern Standard Arabic and fails on Gulf, Egyptian or mixed Arabic-English input, so some groups get worse service.
wr.dialect.platform: Test sets include dialect and code-switched cases, with results reported per language variety.
wr.dialect.manual: Before go-live, have staff run 20 real-style requests in the main dialects your users write in, and record the failures.
wr.holiday.title: Holiday or after-hours approval bypass
wr.holiday.trigger: Some actions need approval, and the service faces the public.
wr.holiday.risk: The approval gate is switched off to clear an Eid, weekend or night backlog and never switched back on.
wr.holiday.platform: Gate changes are logged, need a named approver, and expire automatically.
wr.holiday.manual: Plan cover rosters for holidays; any temporary change is written down with an end date and checked after the holiday.
wr.holiday.evidence: Gate change log with approver and expiry (CTL-HUM-07, CTL-MON-02).
